blocks.text: A motorcyclist is brought in after hitting a car at speed. He is pale, his pelvis looks wrong and his eyes open only when his name is shouted. In the first ten minutes the order in which you act matters more than the diagnosis you eventually reach.

blocks.markdown: **Major trauma** is injury with a significant risk of death or serious disability, and the leading cause of death in young adults in many countries. Deaths cluster at three points: within minutes (catastrophic haemorrhage, airway loss), within hours (haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, intracranial bleeding) and days to weeks (sepsis, multi-organ failure). The emergency department aims to treat the first two groups. Care is delivered by a trauma team using a structured primary survey in the ATLS style, in the UK often written **<C>ABCDE**, with the angle bracket reminding that catastrophic external haemorrhage is dealt with first.

rows: Obstruction, burns to the airway, facial injury
Airway manoeuvres, suction, secure airway; manual in-line stabilisation of the neck
Rate, expansion, percussion, breath sounds, tracheal position
Tension pneumothorax, open chest wound, massive haemothorax, flail chest
Oxygen, decompress a tension pneumothorax, seal and drain
Pulse, blood pressure, capillary refill, pelvis, long bones
Two large-bore IV or intraosseous access, blood products, tranexamic acid, pelvic binder, surgical or radiological haemostasis
Raised intracranial pressure, spinal cord injury
Treat hypoxia and hypotension, neurosurgical referral
blocks.caption: Primary survey in major trauma (doses and protocols to be checked against current ATLS, NICE and local trauma network guidance)

blocks.title: Treat as you find
blocks.text: Do not move on from a letter until the life-threatening problem found there is treated or being treated. Hypotension in trauma is haemorrhage until proved otherwise. Reassess after each intervention, and call for senior and surgical help early.

blocks.title: Primary survey in a road traffic collision
blocks.prompt: A 29-year-old motorcyclist arrives with heart rate 126, blood pressure 78/40, a swollen tender pelvis and no external bleeding. Breath sounds are equal and the trachea is central. Outline the priorities.

steps.text: <C>: no catastrophic external bleeding; proceed. Airway: he is speaking, so patent; maintain manual in-line stabilisation of the cervical spine and give high-flow oxygen.
Breathing: equal breath sounds and central trachea make tension pneumothorax unlikely; look for other chest injury with an eFAST or chest X-ray.

Circulation: shock with a painful pelvis suggests pelvic and intra-abdominal haemorrhage. Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters, gain IV or IO access, send bloods including crossmatch, and start blood product resuscitation (a major haemorrhage protocol). Give tranexamic acid early (as generally taught, within 3 hours of injury; check current dose against local protocol).
Control the source: surgical or interventional radiology haemostasis; call for the trauma team lead and anaesthetist. Do not delay for a CT scan if he remains unstable.

blocks.answer: Pelvic haemorrhage causing shock: binder, blood product resuscitation, tranexamic acid, early surgical or radiological control; maintain cervical spine stabilisation.

blocks.markdown: **Head injury and the Glasgow Coma Scale.** Traumatic brain injury includes a primary injury at impact and **secondary injury** from hypoxia, hypotension, raised intracranial pressure (ICP) or seizures. Preventing secondary injury is the main target in the emergency department. The **Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)** scores eye opening (E, 1 to 4), verbal response (V, 1 to 5) and best motor response (M, 1 to 6); the total ranges from 3 to 15, and the components should always be reported individually.

blocks.caption: GCS total from 3 to 15; CPP: cerebral perfusion pressure in mmHg; MAP: mean arterial pressure; ICP: intracranial pressure

blocks.markdown: The cerebral perfusion pressure falls if MAP falls or ICP rises, which is why hypotension is so harmful in head injury. A patient with a GCS of 8 or less is generally not able to protect the airway, and early intubation by an experienced operator is considered, with cervical spine protection. Imaging decisions follow NICE head injury guidance: a CT head scan is requested within 1 hour for adults with features such as GCS below 13 on initial assessment, GCS below 15 two hours after injury, suspected open or depressed skull fracture, any sign of basal skull fracture (haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leakage, Battle's sign), post-traumatic seizure, focal neurological deficit or more than one vomit. Patients on anticoagulants have lower thresholds, with separate timing rules. Always check the current NICE guideline.

blocks.title: Scoring and deciding on imaging
blocks.prompt: A 45-year-old falls from a ladder. On arrival he opens his eyes to voice, speaks confused sentences and localises to pain. Calculate his GCS and decide on CT imaging.

steps.text: Eye opening to voice scores 3; confused speech scores 4; localising to pain scores 5.
Total GCS = 3 + 4 + 5 = 12, written as E3 V4 M5.
GCS below 13 on initial assessment meets the NICE criterion for CT head within 1 hour (check current guideline), together with CT of the cervical spine if the criteria for imaging are met.
Meanwhile avoid hypoxia and hypotension, give analgesia, and reassess GCS frequently; consider early anaesthetic review if the score falls.

blocks.answer: GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5); CT head within 1 hour; prevent secondary injury and monitor.

blocks.title: Do not blame alcohol
blocks.text: Intoxication can coexist with serious head injury; never attribute reduced consciousness to alcohol without excluding injury, hypoglycaemia and other causes.

blocks.markdown: **Cervical spine injury.** Any patient with a mechanism or findings suggesting neck injury is treated as having an unstable spine until it is cleared. Immobilisation uses manual in-line stabilisation, then a correctly sized collar, blocks and tape, or a vacuum mattress, following local protocol; log-roll with enough staff. Immobilisation must not compromise airway or breathing: a combative patient or one with airway compromise may be better protected by manual stabilisation alone. Clinical decision rules such as the NEXUS criteria or Canadian C-spine rule identify patients who need imaging; CT is the usual imaging in major trauma. Cord injury may show neurological deficit, loss of rectal tone, priapism, or **neurogenic shock**: hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries from loss of sympathetic tone after a high spinal injury.

items: Suspect spinal injury with a high-energy mechanism, neck pain, neurological symptoms, or reduced consciousness.
Maintain alignment during airway management; do not allow the collar to obstruct the airway.
Perform a neurological examination and document it before and after intervention.
Use clinical decision rules (NEXUS or Canadian C-spine rule) or CT according to local pathways.

points: Major trauma care follows <C>ABCDE, treating catastrophic bleeding first and finding and treating life threats at each step.
Hypotension in trauma is haemorrhage until proved otherwise; control the source, give blood products and tranexamic acid early (check doses).
The GCS sums E, V and M components (3 to 15); NICE criteria define CT head within 1 hour; protect against secondary brain injury.
Suspect cervical spine injury in the right mechanism, immobilise sensibly, and recognise neurogenic shock.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a stab wound to the thigh with pulsatile bright red bleeding. He is also making noisy breathing sounds but is conscious. According to the UK <C>ABCDE approach, what should be done first?

options.text: Control the catastrophic bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet
Obtain a CT scan of the head
Insert a urinary catheter
Take a detailed past medical history

questions.correctOptionText: Control the catastrophic bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet

distractorRationale.a: Correct: catastrophic external haemorrhage is treated before airway in the <C>ABCDE approach.
distractorRationale.b: Imaging is not an immediate priority.
distractorRationale.c: Catheterisation is not part of the immediate priorities.
distractorRationale.d: History is secondary to immediate life-saving care.

questions.explanation: Rapid exsanguination can kill faster than airway obstruction, so the UK approach controls catastrophic external bleeding first. Airway management with cervical spine protection follows immediately.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old falls from a roof and is breathless with a blood pressure of 76/40, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation to the right, absent breath sounds on the left and a hyper-resonant left chest. What is the correct immediate action?

options.text: Immediate decompression of the left chest, without waiting for a chest X-ray
Request a chest X-ray first
Give 2 L of fluid and reassess in 30 minutes
Arrange a CT scan of the chest and abdomen

questions.correctOptionText: Immediate decompression of the left chest, without waiting for a chest X-ray

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is a clinical diagnosis of tension pneumothorax which needs immediate decompression.
distractorRationale.b: Delay for imaging may be fatal.
distractorRationale.c: Fluid does not relieve the obstruction.
distractorRationale.d: CT is not appropriate for an unstable patient with a tension pneumothorax.

questions.explanation: The signs indicate a left tension pneumothorax, an obstructive shock caused by rising intrathoracic pressure. It is a clinical diagnosis treated in the Breathing step by decompression followed by chest drain insertion.

questions.stem: Describe the immediate priorities in a trauma patient presenting in haemorrhagic shock, including the approach to circulation, drugs and the importance of source control.
markingGuide: Treats in the <C>ABCDE order with cervical spine protection and oxygen.
Controls external bleeding with direct pressure, tourniquet or packing.
Obtains large-bore IV or intraosseous access and takes bloods including crossmatch; activates the major haemorrhage protocol.
Resuscitates with blood products rather than large volumes of crystalloid.
Gives tranexamic acid early (within 3 hours; dose per local protocol).
Applies a pelvic binder for pelvic injury, uses eFAST or imaging as appropriate.
Emphasises definitive source control by surgery or interventional radiology and avoiding hypothermia.
questions.explanation: Resuscitation only temporises in major haemorrhage; stopping the bleeding is the definitive treatment. Large crystalloid volumes can worsen coagulopathy and hypothermia.

questions.stem: In the Glasgow Coma Scale, a patient who responds to pain with abnormal flexion of the arms (decorticate posture) is scored which motor response?

options.text: M3
M2
M4
M5

distractorRationale.c: M4 is normal withdrawal from pain.

questions.explanation: The motor scale runs from 1 (none) through extension (2), abnormal flexion (3), withdrawal (4), localising (5) to obeying commands (6). Abnormal flexion therefore scores 3.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is brought in after an assault. His GCS is 15 but he has bilateral periorbital bruising and clear fluid dripping from his nose. According to NICE head injury guidance as generally taught, which action is appropriate?

options.text: CT head within 1 hour because of signs of basal skull fracture
Skull X-ray and discharge if normal
Discharge with an advice sheet
Observation only with no imaging

questions.correctOptionText: CT head within 1 hour because of signs of basal skull fracture

distractorRationale.a: Correct: signs of basal skull fracture are a criterion for CT head within 1 hour.
distractorRationale.b: Skull radiographs are not used to exclude intracranial injury.
distractorRationale.c: Discharge is unsafe with these signs.

questions.explanation: Raccoon eyes and CSF rhinorrhoea indicate basal skull fracture, which carries a significant risk of intracranial injury and meningitis. NICE advises CT head promptly regardless of GCS (check the current guideline).

questions.stem: A 25-year-old is ejected from a car in a collision. His GCS is 7 (E2 V2 M3) and he is snoring with intermittent apnoeic pauses. What is the most appropriate airway action?

options.text: Early securing of the airway by an experienced operator with manual in-line neck stabilisation
Place him in the recovery position and observe
Give oral fluids
Wait until the GCS improves before any airway intervention

questions.correctOptionText: Early securing of the airway by an experienced operator with manual in-line neck stabilisation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a GCS of 8 or below with obstruction needs airway protection while the spine is protected.
distractorRationale.b: Recovery position alone is inadequate in a patient with a failing airway and unproven spine.
distractorRationale.c: Oral fluids are unsafe with reduced consciousness.
distractorRationale.d: Waiting risks hypoxia and secondary brain injury.

questions.explanation: A GCS of 8 or less generally means the patient cannot protect the airway, and hypoxia worsens secondary brain injury. Intubation by a skilled operator with cervical spine protection is therefore considered promptly.

questions.stem: A patient opens his eyes only to pain (E2), speaks only inappropriate words (V3) and withdraws from pain (M4). Calculate the total GCS. Give your answer as a score out of 15.
questions.explanation: GCS is the sum of the three components: E2 + V3 + M4 = 9. A score of 9 is a moderate reduction in consciousness, and the components should be reported individually, as E2 V3 M4.

questions.stem: A head-injured patient has a mean arterial pressure of 85 mmHg and an intracranial pressure of 22 mmHg. Calculate the cerebral perfusion pressure. Give your answer in mmHg.
questions.explanation: CPP = MAP - ICP = 85 - 22 = 63 mmHg. A falling MAP or rising ICP reduces CPP, which is why hypotension and raised intracranial pressure must be avoided in head injury; targets are set by the neurocritical care team.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old dives into shallow water and is pulled out unable to move his legs or arms. His blood pressure is 82/48, heart rate 48, and his hands and feet are warm. What is the most likely cause of the haemodynamic findings?

options.text: Neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone after a high cervical cord injury
Haemorrhagic shock from a ruptured spleen
Tension pneumothorax
Cardiogenic shock from myocardial infarction

questions.correctOptionText: Neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone after a high cervical cord injury

distractorRationale.a: Correct: hypotension with bradycardia and warm peripheries after a cord injury indicates neurogenic shock.
distractorRationale.b: Haemorrhage causes tachycardia and cold peripheries, though it must still be excluded.
distractorRationale.c: Tension pneumothorax gives hypotension with respiratory signs and tachycardia.
distractorRationale.d: Myocardial infarction is not suggested by the mechanism.

questions.explanation: A high cord injury interrupts sympathetic outflow, producing vasodilatation and unopposed vagal bradycardia. Because haemorrhage can coexist and cause hypotension, bleeding must still be excluded in any trauma patient.

questions.stem: Discuss the recognition and initial management of a suspected cervical spine injury in a patient who has been in a high-speed collision. Include immobilisation, decision rules and imaging, and the potential hazards of immobilisation.
markingGuide: Recognises risk from mechanism, neck pain or midline tenderness, neurological deficit, reduced consciousness or distracting injuries.
Provides manual in-line stabilisation and then collar, blocks and tape or vacuum mattress per local protocol; log-rolls the patient.
Maintains airway and avoids interrupting airway management for immobilisation.
Performs and documents a neurological examination, including signs of neurogenic shock.
Uses decision rules (NEXUS or Canadian C-spine rule) or CT in line with local trauma network protocols.
Notes hazards of immobilisation such as airway compromise, raised ICP, pressure sores and agitation.
questions.explanation: Spinal protection avoids secondary cord injury, but immobilisation must never compromise airway and breathing. Decision rules reduce unnecessary imaging while identifying those who need it.
